WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT d.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id, app_id
                            ORDER BY downloaded_at, download_id) AS n
  FROM downloads d
), first_dl AS (
  SELECT download_id, account_id, app_id, storefront, downloaded_at
  FROM ranked
  WHERE n = 1
), credited AS (
  SELECT f.app_id, f.storefront, v.source
  FROM first_dl f
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT pv.source
    FROM page_views pv
    WHERE pv.account_id = f.account_id
      AND pv.app_id = f.app_id
      AND pv.storefront = f.storefront
      AND pv.viewed_at <= f.downloaded_at
      AND ({{window_h}} = 0
           OR pv.viewed_at >= f.downloaded_at - make_interval(hours => {{window_h}}))
    ORDER BY pv.viewed_at DESC, pv.view_id DESC
    LIMIT 1
  ) v
), viewers AS (
  SELECT app_id, storefront, source, COUNT(DISTINCT account_id) AS viewers
  FROM page_views
  GROUP BY app_id, storefront, source
), conv AS (
  SELECT app_id, storefront, source, COUNT(*) AS downloads
  FROM credited
  GROUP BY app_id, storefront, source
)
SELECT v.app_id, v.storefront, v.source, v.viewers,
       COALESCE(c.downloads, 0) AS downloads,
       ROUND(COALESCE(c.downloads, 0)::numeric / v.viewers, 4) AS conversion_rate
FROM viewers v
LEFT JOIN conv c
  ON c.app_id = v.app_id AND c.storefront = v.storefront AND c.source = v.source
WHERE v.viewers >= {{min_viewers}}
ORDER BY v.app_id, v.storefront, v.source;

Explanation. Each first-time download then picks exactly one view: the latest at or before it, in its own storefront, inside the window when there is one, with view_id breaking a same-second tie. CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops downloads with no qualifying view, which is the "unattributed" rule. The denominator is computed independently as distinct accounts per page and source, and the credited downloads are LEFT JOINed onto it so sources without conversions stay in the report with 0.

Complexity. One sort for the download ranking, then one index-friendly probe per first-time download (an index on page_views (account_id, app_id, storefront, viewed_at DESC, view_id DESC) makes each probe a short range scan), plus a hash aggregate over views: O(V log V + D log V).

BigQuery: no LATERAL; join first-time downloads to views on the keys and the time condition, then QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY download_id ORDER BY viewed_at DESC, view_id DESC) = 1; TIMESTAMP_SUB(downloaded_at, INTERVAL {{window_h}} HOUR). Snowflake: QUALIFY the same way, or LATERAL with a correlated subquery (supported in limited forms); DATEADD(hour, -{{window_h}}, downloaded_at). Spark SQL: a join plus row_number() in a subquery; downloaded_at - INTERVAL {{window_h}} HOURS. MySQL 8: LATERAL is supported from 8.0.14; otherwise the join-and-rank form; DATE_SUB(downloaded_at, INTERVAL {{window_h}} HOUR).

Edge cases built into the data. Several views from different sources before a download; downloads before any view (unattributed); downloads between two views; a view in the download's second; re-downloads days later after another look at the page; groups with no conversions. Hard: views exactly {{window_h}} hours before the download (credited) and one second older (unattributed); an earlier download in a second storefront. Very Hard: the same download logged twice in one second; two views in one second from different sources; groups below the floor.

Counting every download; partitioning the first-download ranking by storefront; crediting the first view; COUNT(*) of views as the denominator; < instead of <= on the view time or the window; an INNER JOIN that loses zero rows; NOT EXISTS (earlier download with downloaded_at <) which keeps both copies of a duplicated download; tie-breaking views by the lowest view_id; integer division.

(2) Report models side by side with their definitions; first-touch credits discovery, last-touch credits the final nudge; disagreements are expected and not errors. (3) Aggregate counts only, with a minimum group size or added noise, no cross-session linking; report signed-out traffic as its own segment. WITH ev AS (
  SELECT e.*,
         SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_type IN ('renewed', 'expired') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY e.subscription_id ORDER BY e.event_ts, e.event_id
                 ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS grp
  FROM billing_events e
), opened AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (subscription_id, grp)
         subscription_id, grp, plan_id, event_ts AS start_ts
  FROM ev
  WHERE event_type = 'renewal_failed'
  ORDER BY subscription_id, grp, event_ts, event_id
), episodes AS (
  SELECT o.plan_id, s.storefront, p.grace_days, o.start_ts,
         c.event_type AS closed_by, c.event_ts AS closed_ts
  FROM opened o
  JOIN subscriptions s ON s.subscription_id = o.subscription_id
  JOIN plans p ON p.plan_id = o.plan_id
  LEFT JOIN ev c
    ON c.subscription_id = o.subscription_id
   AND c.grp = o.grp + 1
   AND c.event_type IN ('renewed', 'expired')
  WHERE o.start_ts + make_interval(days => {{n_days}}) <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{as_of}}'
), flagged AS (
  SELECT plan_id, storefront,
         COALESCE(closed_by = 'renewed'
                  AND closed_ts <= start_ts + make_interval(days => {{n_days}}), false) AS rec,
         COALESCE(closed_by = 'renewed' AND grace_days > 0
                  AND closed_ts <= start_ts + make_interval(days => grace_days), false) AS in_grace
  FROM episodes
)
SELECT plan_id, storefront,
       COUNT(*)                                   AS entered,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rec)                AS recovered,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rec AND in_grace)   AS recovered_in_grace,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE rec)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS recovery_rate
FROM flagged
GROUP BY plan_id, storefront
ORDER BY plan_id, storefront;

Explanation. The running count of closing events (renewed or expired) splits each subscription's history into stretches; a stretch's first renewal_failed opens an episode, and later failures in the same stretch are retry attempts. The closing event that ends the stretch carries the next count, which is how the episode finds its close without a correlated subquery; an open episode has no such row and stays unrecovered through the LEFT JOIN. A renewed before any failure is in a stretch with no failure and recovers nothing; after an expired, a new purchase's renewed sits in a stretch with no failure too. The window is measured from the opening failure, so the grace period is inside it; both comparisons are on timestamps with intervals, inclusive. The maturity filter (start + {{n_days}} days <= as_of) only removes episodes in Very Hard rounds. The plan is the one on the opening failure.

Complexity. One sort per subscription for the window function (O(E log E) overall), a DISTINCT ON sort and a hash join: near-linear in events. Partitioning by subscription parallelises cleanly.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: the same running SUM window; QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY subscription_id, grp ORDER BY event_ts, event_id) = 1 for DISTINCT ON; TIMESTAMP_ADD(start_ts, INTERVAL {{n_days}} DAY) (and an INTERVAL grace_days DAY with a column is allowed); COUNTIF. Snowflake: QUALIFY, DATEADD(day, {{n_days}}, start_ts), COUNT_IF; CONDITIONAL_TRUE_EVENT(event_type IN ('renewed','expired')) is a compact alternative to the running sum. Spark SQL: sum(...) over (...), row_number() in a subquery, start_ts + make_interval(0, 0, 0, grace_days). MySQL 8: window functions are available; DATE_ADD(start_ts, INTERVAL grace_days DAY); SUM(CASE …) instead of FILTER.

Edge cases built into the data. Retry attempts inside an episode; recoveries inside the grace period, after it but inside the window, and after the window; expiries; episodes still open; a plan with no grace period; ordinary renewals before failures. Hard: several episodes per subscription; recoveries exactly at grace_days and exactly at {{n_days}} days (counted) and one second after; a purchase after an expiry. Very Hard: plan changes between episodes; an episode exactly {{n_days}} days old on as_of (counted) and one a day younger (left out).

Common mistakes. Counting every renewal_failed as an entry; taking the next event (LEAD) as the close when it is another failure; starting the window at the end of the grace period; any later renewed counted as a recovery, including after expiry or after the window; comparing dates instead of timestamps; COUNT(DISTINCT subscription_id) (a subscription can enter retry twice); the subscription's latest plan; including immature episodes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Recent cohorts have not had their full window, so their recovery is right-censored; show only mature cohorts, or show recent ones with "so far" and a survival curve. (2) Compare cohorts entering just before and after the change (with seasonality controls such as last year's same period), or an experiment where the setting differs by app or storefront; state the confounders. (3) Key notifications by a unique notification or transaction id, upsert raw events, and rebuild episodes for affected subscriptions from the ordered raw events, so arrival order never matters. (4) Keep per-subscription state (open episode start, plan) and apply each day's events in order; only subscriptions with new events are touched, and closed episodes are immutable.

Rubric anchors. 2: right structure, but every failure counted, or the window measured from the end of grace. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also handles cohort maturity, the measurement of a grace-period change and idempotent ingestion credibly.

Strong signals. Draws the state machine (not in retry → in retry → closed) before writing SQL; asks whether grace is inside the window; tests the exact boundary. Red flags. A self-join of every failure with every later renewal; treating the episode count as subscriptions; stating the exercise's retry or grace lengths as a store's actual policy.

WITH listens AS (
  SELECT listener_id, track_id, MIN(played_at) AS first_listen
  FROM plays
  WHERE ms_played >= {{min_ms}}
  GROUP BY listener_id, track_id
), first_add AS (
  SELECT listener_id, track_id, MIN(added_at) AS added_at
  FROM library_adds
  GROUP BY listener_id, track_id
), pairs AS (
  SELECT l.listener_id, l.track_id,
         (a.added_at IS NOT NULL
          AND a.added_at <= l.first_listen + INTERVAL '7 days') AS added
  FROM listens l
  LEFT JOIN first_add a
    ON a.listener_id = l.listener_id AND a.track_id = l.track_id
  WHERE a.added_at IS NULL OR a.added_at >= l.first_listen
)
SELECT g.genre,
       COUNT(DISTINCT p.listener_id)          AS listeners,
       COUNT(*)                               AS pairs,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.added)        AS added,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE p.added)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS add_rate
FROM pairs p
JOIN track_genres g ON g.track_id = p.track_id
GROUP BY g.genre
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.listener_id) >= {{min_listeners}}
ORDER BY add_rate DESC, g.genre;

Explanation. Everything is decided at the pair grain. The first listen ignores previews (below the threshold), so a preview neither starts the clock nor makes an add "after listening". The earliest add is the only add that matters: before the first listen means the track was already saved, and the pair leaves both the numerator and the denominator (the WHERE runs before aggregation); otherwise the add counts if it is within seven days, inclusive at both ends. Pairs join to genres last, so a track in two genres contributes to both, and the floor counts distinct listeners, not pairs.

Complexity. Two hash aggregates (plays and adds) and a hash join at the pair grain, then a small aggregate per genre: O(P + A). At scale, the pair table is the one to keep incrementally.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_ADD(first_listen, INTERVAL 7 DAY), COUNTIF(added), COUNT(DISTINCT …) is exact (use APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT only if approximate is acceptable, which it is not for a floor). Snowflake: DATEADD(day, 7, first_listen), COUNT_IF. Spark SQL: first_listen + INTERVAL 7 DAYS, count_if. MySQL 8: DATE_ADD(first_listen, INTERVAL 7 DAY), SUM(added) with booleans as integers.

Edge cases built into the data. Adds in the same second as the first listen and exactly seven days later (both count) and one second after (does not); adds before the first listen, some followed by another add later; pairs never added; adds of tracks never played; a small genre whose pair count reaches the floor while its listener count does not. Hard: previews before the first listen, previews of exactly min_ms - 1 ms and listens of exactly min_ms ms; adds after a preview but before the first listen (excluded); tracks only previewed (no pair); a track re-added weeks later. Very Hard: tracks in two genres.

Common mistakes. Keeping pre-added pairs as "not added"; using the latest or any add; an exclusive window; starting the clock at a preview; flooring on pairs; counting a two-genre track once; an INNER JOIN to adds that drops pairs never added; ordering by the unrounded value with a different tie-break; integer division.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Album: the pair is listener × album, the first listen is the first qualifying play of any of its tracks; the add is the album or any of its tracks, which must be defined. (2) Use play time for the clock but process by arrival, recompute pairs touched by late plays, and freeze published numbers after a stated lateness bound (or publish revisions). (3) A listener floor limits re-identification of individuals but not of small cohorts in small storefronts; add storefront-level minimums, suppression of complementary cells and, if needed, noise. (4) Keep a pair table with first listen and earliest add, update it from each day's new plays and adds with LEAST, and recompute only genres touched.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape, but pre-added pairs kept or the floor on pairs. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also discusses late plays, privacy floors beyond a count, and the incremental pair table.

Strong signals. Asks what happens to tracks saved before the first listen; reduces to the pair grain before joining genres. Red flags. Joining every play to every add; averaging per-listener rates without saying so; claiming the listen threshold is a real service's rule.

from bisect import bisect_right


def current_lines(lines, positions, duration_ms=None):
    shown = {}                          # start -> index of the line listed last with that start
    for i, (start, _end) in enumerate(lines):
        shown[start] = i
    starts = sorted(shown)
    index = [shown[s] for s in starts]
    ends = [lines[i][1] for i in index]
    out = []
    for p in positions:
        if duration_ms:
            p %= duration_ms
        k = bisect_right(starts, p) - 1     # the last start at or before p
        out.append(index[k] if k >= 0 and p < ends[k] else -1)
    return out

Explanation. Lines (after corrections) do not overlap, so at any position the only line that can be on screen is the one with the largest start at or before it. A dict filled in input order resolves corrections (the later listing overwrites the earlier one), sorting the surviving starts once gives a searchable array, and bisect_right(starts, p) - 1 finds the candidate in O(log n): bisect_right puts a position equal to a start on that line. The half-open end check turns a gap or a line's exact end into -1. Repeat-one positions are reduced modulo the duration first, so a position equal to duration_ms is the start of the song.

Complexity. O(n log n) to sort, O(log n) per position: O((n + q) log n) time, O(n) memory. The timing test (50 000 lines, 200 000 positions with a seek about every 8 samples) runs in well under a second; checking every line per position is 10¹⁰ steps, and a forward-moving pointer that resets on each backward seek still walks about 6 × 10⁸ lines (over 40 s in CPython).

Common mistakes. bisect_left (a position exactly at a start gets the previous line); closed intervals (a line still shown at its end); returning the index into the sorted list; keeping the first of two lines with the same start; forgetting that a correction can be shorter and leave a gap; a pointer that assumes positions only move forward; wrapping with p % duration_ms only when p > duration_ms (misses p == duration_ms).

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep the current index and check starts[k] <= p < starts[k+1] first (the usual case during playback), falling back to a binary search on a seek. (2) An interval tree or a sorted list of starts with a max-end augmentation returns all k covering intervals in O(log n + k); for a handful of overlapping singers, one sorted list per singer is simpler. (3) Shift positions by the offset rather than every line (p - offset), keeping integer milliseconds so boundaries stay exact. (4) Per-song jobs are embarrassingly parallel; compare line starts with detected vocal onsets and report the median and spread of the offset, flagging files beyond a threshold.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct output with a scan per position, or an off-by-one at the boundaries. 3: correct with one sort and binary search, with a clear complexity argument. 4: also discusses the playback fast path, overlapping lines and batch timing quality credibly.

Strong signals. Asks whether intervals are half-open and whether positions can go backwards; mentions bisect_right versus bisect_left deliberately. Red flags. Sorting the positions and returning them in sorted order; mutating lines and losing the original indexes.

import calendar
from datetime import date


def renewals(plans, subs, as_of):
    end = date.fromisoformat(as_of)

    def on(month_index, day):                 # the anchor day, clamped to the month's last day
        y, m = divmod(month_index, 12)
        return date(y, m + 1, min(day, calendar.monthrange(y, m + 1)[1]))

    def first_after(start, day, months, t):   # first renewal strictly after t, in O(1)
        k = max(1, (t.year * 12 + t.month - 1 - start) // months)
        d = on(start + k * months, day)
        if d <= t:
            d = on(start + (k + 1) * months, day)
        return d

    out = []
    for purchase, plan, changes in subs:
        p = date.fromisoformat(purchase)
        if p > end:
            out.append(None)
            continue
        start, day = p.year * 12 + p.month - 1, p.day
        pending = pending_at = None
        for when, new in changes:
            c = date.fromisoformat(when)
            if c > end:
                break
            if pending is not None and pending_at <= c:          # that renewal came first
                start = pending_at.year * 12 + pending_at.month - 1
                plan, pending = pending, None
            if plans[new][0] > plans[plan][0]:                   # upgrade: a new period today
                plan, pending = new, None
                start, day = c.year * 12 + c.month - 1, c.day
            elif plans[new][0] < plans[plan][0]:                 # downgrade: at the next renewal
                pending = new
                pending_at = first_after(start, day, plans[plan][1], c)
            else:                                                # kept the plan in effect
                pending = None
        if pending is not None and pending_at <= end:
            start = pending_at.year * 12 + pending_at.month - 1
            plan, pending = pending, None
        if pending is not None:
            out.append((pending_at.isoformat(), pending))
        else:
            out.append((first_after(start, day, plans[plan][1], end).isoformat(), plan))
    return out

Explanation. A schedule is three numbers: the period start as a month index, the anchor day and the period length. Renewal k is in month start + k × months on the clamped anchor day, so renewals never drift (31 January → 28 February → 31 March), and the first renewal after any date is found directly: (month_index(t) - start) // months lands on the renewal in or before t's month, and at most one step forward fixes the same-month case. Changes are applied in date order; a pending downgrade is resolved first if its renewal falls on or before the change date (renewals come before same-day changes), then the change is compared with the plan really in effect. An upgrade resets the schedule to the change date; a downgrade records its effective renewal (which cannot move, because no renewal falls between the request and it); re-choosing the plan in effect cancels it. Whatever is still pending at as_of is exactly the next renewal, with the new plan.

Complexity. O(1) per subscription plus O(1) per change, O(n + c) overall; memory O(n) for the output. The timing test (150 000 subscriptions with synthetic purchases since 1980, mostly monthly) runs in about a second; stepping renewal by renewal is around 5 × 10⁷ date computations (close to a minute in CPython).

Common mistakes. import calendar
from datetime import date


def renewals(plans, subs, as_of):
    end = date.fromisoformat(as_of)

    def on(month_index, day):                 # the anchor day, clamped to the month's last day
        y, m = divmod(month_index, 12)
        return date(y, m + 1, min(day, calendar.monthrange(y, m + 1)[1]))

    def first_after(start, day, months, t):   # first renewal strictly after t, in O(1)
        k = max(1, (t.year * 12 + t.month - 1 - start) // months)
        d = on(start + k * months, day)
        if d <= t:
            d = on(start + (k + 1) * months, day)
        return d

    out = []
    for purchase, plan, changes in subs:
        p = date.fromisoformat(purchase)
        if p > end:
            out.append(None)
            continue
        start, day = p.year * 12 + p.month - 1, p.day
        pending = pending_at = None
        for when, new in changes:
            c = date.fromisoformat(when)
            if c > end:
                break
            if pending is not None and pending_at <= c:          # that renewal came first
                start = pending_at.year * 12 + pending_at.month - 1
                plan, pending = pending, None
            if plans[new][0] > plans[plan][0]:                   # upgrade: a new period today
                plan, pending = new, None
                start, day = c.year * 12 + c.month - 1, c.day
            elif plans[new][0] < plans[plan][0]:                 # downgrade: at the next renewal
                pending = new
                pending_at = first_after(start, day, plans[plan][1], c)
            else:                                                # kept the plan in effect
                pending = None
        if pending is not None and pending_at <= end:
            start = pending_at.year * 12 + pending_at.month - 1
            plan, pending = pending, None
        if pending is not None:
            out.append((pending_at.isoformat(), pending))
        else:
            out.append((first_after(start, day, plans[plan][1], end).isoformat(), plan))
    return out

def group_near_duplicates(photos, max_bits, keep_best=False):
    score = {}
    hashes = {}
    for pid, h, s in photos:
        if h is not None:
            hashes[pid] = h
            score[pid] = s
    ids = sorted(hashes)
    hs = [hashes[p] for p in ids]
    n = len(ids)
    parent = list(range(n))

    def find(a):
        while parent[a] != a:
            parent[a] = parent[parent[a]]
            a = parent[a]
        return a

    # Pigeonhole: split the 64 bits into max_bits + 1 blocks. Two hashes within
    # max_bits of each other agree exactly on at least one block.
    blocks = max_bits + 1
    edges = [64 * b // blocks for b in range(blocks + 1)]
    for b in range(blocks):
        lo, hi = edges[b], edges[b + 1]
        mask = ((1 << (hi - lo)) - 1) << lo
        buckets = {}
        for i, h in enumerate(hs):
            key = h & mask
            if key in buckets:
                buckets[key].append(i)
            else:
                buckets[key] = [i]
        for members in buckets.values():
            m = len(members)
            if m < 2:
                continue
            for x in range(m):
                i = members[x]
                hi_ = hs[i]
                for y in range(x + 1, m):
                    j = members[y]
                    ri, rj = find(i), find(j)
                    if ri != rj and bin(hi_ ^ hs[j]).count("1") <= max_bits:
                        if ri < rj:
                            parent[rj] = ri
                        else:
                            parent[ri] = rj

    groups = {}
    for i in range(n):
        groups.setdefault(find(i), []).append(ids[i])     # ids ascending within a group
    out = sorted((g for g in groups.values() if len(g) >= 2), key=lambda g: g[0])
    if not keep_best:
        return out
    result = []
    for g in out:
        keeper = min(g, key=lambda p: (-score[p], p))
        result.append([keeper] + [p for p in g if p != keeper])
    return result

Explanation. If two 64-bit hashes differ in at most d bits, cut both into d + 1 contiguous blocks. The d differing bits fall into at most d blocks, so at least one block is identical in both hashes (the pigeonhole principle). For each block position, bucket the photos by that block's value; any near-duplicate pair shares at least one bucket. Inside a bucket, confirm a pair with an exact bit count of the XOR. Union-find merges confirmed pairs into groups, and a pair already in one set is skipped before the bit count. Photos without a hash are left out and a repeated id is collapsed by building a dict first. Groups are read back from the union-find roots, ids ascend inside each group because the indices follow the sorted ids, and groups are sorted by their first, smallest id. With keep_best, the keeper is the minimum of (-score, id), which is the highest score with the smaller id on a tie, and the group order is still decided by the smallest id.

Complexity. Bucketing is O(n · (d + 1)). The pair work is the sum over buckets of the bucket size squared. For uniformly spread hashes a block of b = 64 / (d + 1) bits gives n / 2ᵇ photos per bucket, so for d = 4 (13-bit blocks) and n = 40 000 it is about 5 photos per bucket, plus the members of real clusters. The timing test (40 000 photos, d = 4) runs in about 0.7 s in CPython, and d = 3 in about 0.3 s. All pairs is 8 × 10⁸ XOR-and-count steps, over a minute and a half in CPython. As d grows the blocks shrink and buckets fill (d = 12 gives 5-bit blocks and n / 32 photos per bucket), so the method is for small d.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++, hashes are unsigned 64-bit values: Java has no unsigned long, but XOR and Long.bitCount work on the raw bits, so the sign never matters; in C++ use uint64_t and std::popcount (or __builtin_popcountll). In SQL engines, BigQuery has BIT_COUNT on INT64, and Spark has bit_count; a self-join on each block value followed by a bit count is the distributed form of the same idea, and the connected components then need an iterative job or a graph library. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Exactly max_bits differing bits; max_bits + 1; a chain A ~ B ~ C with A and C 2·max_bits apart; a photo with no near duplicate; an empty library; max_bits = 0, where only identical hashes group; differences in bit 63 and bit 0; groups ordered by their smallest id; (Hard) a photo without a hash, a photo listed twice in a group, and a photo listed twice with no near duplicate (it must not form a group with itself); (Very Hard) the keeper by highest score, a score tie broken by the smaller id, and groups ordered by their smallest id rather than by their keeper.

Common mistakes. Comparing all pairs; sorting by hash and comparing neighbours (misses pairs that differ in high bits); blocks that do not cover all 64 bits, or 8 fixed bytes, which is only correct for d ≤ 7 and wasteful for small d; treating near duplicates as non-transitive (pair lists instead of groups); a repeated photo id grouped with itself; None hashes crashing the XOR; recursive DFS over a long chain; ordering groups by their keeper.

Options: fewer, wider blocks with a second-level search (allowing a few errors per block and enumerating neighbours of the block value), multi-probe hashing, or an index such as a BK-tree for moderate sizes; accept answers that quantify the bucket sizes. (2) Keep the block buckets and the union-find; a new photo is bucketed d + 1 times and compared only with its buckets' members. Deletions break union-find, so rebuild the affected group from its members, or keep explicit edges for small groups. (3) Pick a representative per group (for example the best score) and require members to be within d of it, a clustering with a centre; or cut chains with a maximum diameter. It costs more comparisons and can leave photos ungrouped. (4) Emit (block index, block value, photo) rows, group by the first two, emit candidate pairs, confirm with a bit count, and run connected components (iterative label propagation or a union-find per partition followed by a merge). Skew on popular block values needs salting or a cap.

MOD = 1_000_000_007
BASE = 257


def _chunks(data, window, mask, min_size, max_size):
    """Yield (offset, length) of each content-defined chunk of data."""
    out = []
    n = len(data)
    top = pow(BASE, window - 1, MOD)       # weight of the byte leaving the window
    limit = max_size if max_size is not None else n + 1
    h = 0
    start = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if i >= window:
            h = (h - data[i - window] * top) % MOD
        h = (h * BASE + data[i]) % MOD
        length = i - start + 1
        if length == limit or (i >= window - 1 and length >= min_size and h & mask == 0):
            out.append((start, length))
            start = i + 1
    if start < n:
        out.append((start, n - start))
    return out


def delta_chunks(installed, new, window, mask_bits, min_size=1, max_size=None):
    mask = (1 << mask_bits) - 1
    have = set()
    for f in installed:
        for off, length in _chunks(f, window, mask, min_size, max_size):
            have.add(f[off:off + length])
    mine = _chunks(new, window, mask, min_size, max_size)
    download = []
    for off, length in mine:
        piece = new[off:off + length]
        if piece not in have:
            have.add(piece)
            download.append((off, length))
    return (len(mine), download)

Explanation. The window hash is a polynomial in base 257 over the last window bytes, so it rolls: subtract the outgoing byte times 257^(window − 1), multiply by 257, add the incoming byte, all modulo the prime. The outgoing weight is computed once with pow(257, window - 1, MOD). Python's % returns a non-negative value after the subtraction. The hash is updated for every byte of the file, independently of where chunks start, so it is defined from position window − 1 onwards and can reach into the previous chunk. A chunk ends after byte i when it has reached max_size, or when the window is full, the chunk has at least min_size bytes and the low mask_bits bits of the hash are zero. The rest of the file after the last cut is the final chunk. Installed files are chunked first into a set of their chunk bytes. The new file's chunks are then walked once: a chunk not in the set is downloaded and added to the set, so a repeat inside the update is downloaded once.

Complexity. O(n) hash updates over all bytes, plus O(total chunk bytes) for slicing and hashing the chunks into the set. The timing test hashes about 2 MB (1 MB installed, about 1 MB new) with a 64-byte window in about 1.0 s in CPython. Recomputing each window is O(n · window), about 130 million multiply-and-mod steps, roughly 10–12 s in CPython even with map and sum doing the inner loop. The base 257 is deliberate: int.from_bytes computes a base-256 value in C, which would be a different hash.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ keep the hash in a 64-bit integer: with a prime near 10⁹, h * 257 + b fits easily. After subtracting the outgoing term, add the modulus before taking %, because % keeps the sign of the dividend in both languages. Production chunkers often use a Rabin fingerprint over GF(2) or a gear hash, which roll with shifts and XORs instead of multiplication; the boundaries differ but the algorithm is the same. A SQL formulation is impractical. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. An empty update; an unchanged file (nothing to download); a file shorter than the window; an insertion near the start, after which later chunks are found again; a passage moved to the front; two boundaries fewer than window bytes apart, which needs the window to run over the whole file; (Hard) a run of one repeated byte, cut only at max_size, with the identical chunks downloaded once; a hash boundary inside the first min_size bytes, ignored; a chunk of exactly max_size bytes; (Very Hard) chunks found in a second installed file; a passage repeated inside the update; no installed files at all.

Common mistakes. Restarting the window at each chunk start; testing the hash before the window is full; > instead of >= for min_size, or cutting at max_size + 1; forgetting the final chunk, or emitting an empty final chunk; offsets into the installed file instead of into new; downloading a repeated chunk twice; recomputing each window; using int.from_bytes or Python's hash() as the boundary hash; a negative intermediate value in languages where % keeps the sign.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Fixed blocks shift after an insertion, so every block after it changes. Content-defined boundaries depend only on the bytes in the window, so after the edit the same boundaries reappear and only the chunks that overlap the edit change. (2) The expected chunk size is about 2^mask_bits bytes (plus the minimum); smaller chunks find more reuse but cost more metadata and requests, and min_size and max_size bound the extremes. For a 2 GB game, expected chunks of tens of KB to a few MB are reasonable; justify by metadata size versus wasted bytes per edit. (3) Precompute each version's chunk list and digests once; a device sends its installed version (or its chunk digests, compactly), the service answers with the list of missing chunk digests, and chunks are served from a content-addressed store and a CDN. (4) Compression and encryption destroy byte-level similarity. Chunk before compressing (compress each chunk), keep assets as separate files, or encrypt per chunk with a deterministic, convergent scheme only where that is acceptable.

from datetime import date


def _days_between(a, b):
    return (date.fromisoformat(b) - date.fromisoformat(a)).days


def _half_up(num, den):
    return (2 * num + den) // (2 * den)          # num, den >= 0


def proceeds_report(transactions):
    first_sale = {}     # (subscriber, product) -> date of the earliest sale
    sales = {}          # txn -> what a refund needs
    rows = {}
    for t in transactions:
        if t["type"] == "sale":
            key = (t["subscriber"], t["product"])
            first_sale.setdefault(key, t["date"])
            net = _half_up(t["price"] * 10000, 10000 + t["tax_bp"])     # the price includes the tax
            days = _days_between(first_sale[key], t["date"])
            rate = 15 if days >= 365 else 30                             # 365 days or more
            proceeds = net - _half_up(net * rate, 100)                   # half up, not to even
            row = rows.setdefault((t["app"], t["currency"]), [t["app"], t["currency"], 0, 0])
            row[2] += 1
            row[3] += proceeds
            sales[t["txn"]] = {"row": row, "proceeds": proceeds, "refunded": False}
        elif t["type"] == "refund":
            sale = sales.get(t["original"])
            if sale is None or sale["refunded"]:
                continue
            sale["row"][2] -= 1
            sale["row"][3] -= sale["proceeds"]                           # reverse exactly what the sale paid
            sale["refunded"] = True
    return sorted(rows.values())

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Tax treated as added on top. price - price * tax_bp // 10000 removes a percentage of the tax-inclusive price, which is more than the tax actually included. Symptom: proceeds in VAT storefronts are too low (a 999 sale with 19% included nets 810 instead of 839). Fix: divide the tax out, price × 10000 / (10000 + tax_bp), rounded half up.
  2. The reduced rate starts a day late. days > 365 charges the full rate on the anniversary itself. Symptom: renewals on day 365 pay 30%. Fix: >= 365.
  3. Banker's rounding. round(net * rate / 100) uses Python's round-half-to-even on a float. For 995 at 30% it gives 298 instead of 299, so proceeds are one minor unit too high whenever the commission is an exact half with an even floor. Fix: integer half-up, (2 * num + den) // (2 * den).
  4. A refund recomputes the commission at its own date. A refund dated after the subscriber's anniversary uses 15%, so it takes back more than the sale (charged at 30%) paid. Symptom: proceeds drop by more than the refunded sale earned. Fix: store the sale's proceeds and subtract exactly that.
  5. Rows keyed by storefront. Two storefronts that share a currency (for example two eurozone storefronts) produce two rows for one app and currency. Symptom: duplicate currency rows, and payment totals that do not match. Fix: key rows by (app, currency).

Each bug has its own check, and every other check passes with that bug alone left in: a tax-inclusive sale, a sale exactly 365 days after the first, a commission of exactly half a minor unit, a refund after the anniversary of a sale made before it, and two storefronts that share a currency (that check sets tax_bp to 0 so that it isolates the key). Three further checks guard against over-fixing: a sale 364 days after the first stays at 30%, a second refund and a refund of an unknown sale change nothing, and each product has its own first year.

The payment key is the currency, not the storefront. A refund is a reversal of a stored result, never a recalculation, because the inputs to the calculation (here the rate, in reality also tax rates and exchange rates) can change between the sale and the refund.

(2) Each transaction carries the tax rate (and ideally the tax amount) that applied at sale time; reports are rebuilt from stored transactions, never by looking up today's rates. Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • On the device. For each opted-in app, the device keeps a daily record: launches and a launch-time histogram with fixed bucket edges; foreground and background time and an energy estimate in coarse buckets; crash count and, per crash, a compact report with the app version, the OS version, the model family, an exception type and the stack as binary image identifiers and offsets. It never sends content, location, account or advertising identifiers, or other apps' data. At upload, the record becomes a report with a random identifier for that report only, the day, and coarse attributes.
  • Ingestion. An upload endpoint authenticates the device as a genuine opted-in device class without identifying it (for example with an anonymous token issued per day), validates the schema and size, and writes reports to a durable log partitioned by app. The random report identifier makes a re-sent report idempotent. Late reports (devices offline for days) land in their own day's partition until a cut-off, after which they are dropped.
  • Symbolication. Crash stacks are stored unsymbolicated with the binary image identifier (build UUID) and offsets. A symbolication service applies the developer's symbol files when they exist; when symbols arrive later, a reprocessing job symbolicates the retained raw crashes for that build.
  • Grouping. A signature is computed from the top frames of the crashing thread after symbolication, normalised (inlined frames, system frames trimmed); before symbolication, the binary image and offsets give a provisional key. Regrouping after symbols arrive maps provisional keys to signatures so that counts are continuous.
  • Aggregation. Per app, version, OS, model family and day: device-days (reports), launches, merged launch-time histograms (percentiles read from the merged histogram), crash counts, crashing device-days, energy buckets. Crash rate is defined explicitly, for example crashes per 1 000 sessions or the share of device-days with a crash.
  • Release rule. A cell is published only if at least {{min_devices}} reports contributed. Cells below the threshold are merged upward (model family into "all models", day into week). To stop subtraction attacks, publish only from a fixed hierarchy of cells and suppress complementary cells when a sibling differs from its parent by fewer than {{min_devices}} reports, or round counts and percentiles.
  • Retention. Raw reports are kept for a short, stated period (long enough for late symbols and reprocessing), then deleted. Aggregates are kept longer. An opt-out stops collection on the device immediately; earlier reports cannot be linked to it and expire with the raw data.
  • Freshness. Daily batch aggregation, with a first publication for a new version as soon as its cells pass the threshold, and a visible "data so far" label.

Competing designs to accept. Streaming aggregation of reports as they arrive (fine if the release rule is applied at publication, not at ingestion); server-side sketches such as t-digest or DDSketch instead of fixed histograms (fine if mergeable and the device still does not send raw values); adding calibrated noise to released counts as well as thresholds (a strong answer, if it says what it costs in accuracy). Designs that keep a stable device id "for deduplication" do not meet the constraints.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A launch-crash spike multiplying volume for one app; symbol files missing or uploaded late; signatures that split with compiler or OS changes; a crash-rate denominator that changes when uploads fail (rates jump while counts do not); thresholds that hide small apps entirely; overlapping cells that allow subtraction; late reports changing published numbers without notice.

  • Launch crash on one model family, 30 times the usual crash volume: the log is partitioned by app, so other apps are isolated; autoscale the symbolication and grouping stage for that app, or sample the stacks for grouping while counting every crash exactly. Publish the count early, because the cell is far above {{min_devices}}, and let the developer see the signature by model family. Check that ingestion quotas were per app, not global.
  • Crash rate doubled but no new signature and report count halved: suspect the denominator. Fewer daily reports (for example an OS update that delayed uploads, or an upload rejection after a schema change) means fewer device-days with launches but crash reports still arriving separately. Compare reports per version over time, check rejection metrics, hold the published rate with a data-quality flag, and fix the join so that numerator and denominator come from the same reports.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Show counts by provisional signature (binary image and offsets) with a "symbols missing" banner; when symbols arrive, reprocess the retained raw crashes and remap provisional keys, so the history is continuous. (2) The difference of two cells reveals a group of three devices. Publish only from a fixed hierarchy, suppress cells whose complement is below the threshold, or add noise; say which and what it costs. (3) Publish at a coarser grain (all models, the week so far) until finer cells pass, and label the numbers as early; never lower the threshold for new versions. (4) Normalise frames (strip compiler-generated suffixes, inline frames) and keep a mapping table from old to new signatures, so a split is merged and trends stay continuous.

  • Events.
