The product page reads a small cache refreshed {{freshness}}.
  • Per version. Counts per star by the version stored on the current rating, so a changed rating moves from the old version to the new one. A daily snapshot of current state by version gives developers history; an event-based view gives "ratings submitted per day per version".
  • Rebuild. Every derived table is a deterministic function of the event log. A rebuild replays events into a new table version, compares it with the live one, and swaps atomically. A periodic consistency check recomputes summaries for a sample of apps and alerts on any difference.
  • Privacy. Developer-facing views carry the display name and review text only; customer ids stay in internal tables. Account closure removes the customer's ratings and reviews from current state and summaries and replaces the identifier in the log with a tombstone, per the exercise's rule.

Competing designs to accept. A streaming job maintaining per-star counts in a key-value store, with a nightly batch recomputation that corrects drift; a database with transactional updates of current state and summary counts in one transaction (fine at {{ratings_per_day}} if partitioned by app); a lakehouse with MERGE into current state and summaries rebuilt hourly (fine if it meets {{freshness}}). Each must keep summaries equal to a recomputation.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Hot apps after a release concentrating writes on one partition; running averages that drift and cannot be corrected; replays that double-apply changes without sequence checks; removals implemented as deletes, so appeals cannot restore; resets that mutate ratings; per-version numbers that count a customer twice after a change; caches that are not invalidated per storefront.

Incident guidance.

  • Ten times the usual rating rate for an hour in one storefront: writes concentrate on one app's partition. Absorb them in the log, and update the summary from per-partition pre-aggregates (sum the per-star deltas in micro-batches) rather than one update per rating; the summary lag recovers without losing events. Alert on summary lag against {{freshness}}, and split hot apps across sub-partitions merged at read.
  • Reset in all {{storefronts}} storefronts; a few still show the old rating an hour later: the reset events were applied, but cached summaries in a few storefronts were not refreshed, or the reset was processed before some ratings that arrived out of order. Check the cache invalidation per storefront and the reset's position in the event order, recompute those summaries from current state, and add a check that the cache's reset_at matches the table's.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Apply removals as events in order; each subtracts one rating from the summary in the same transaction or micro-batch that updates the review state; the page shows the old summary until the batch's update is published, within {{freshness}}. (2) Replay from the event log into new tables with sequence checks, compare with the live tables per app and storefront, swap, and record the correction; prove it with a full recomputation of the counts. (3) Compare the rating distribution of ratings submitted or changed while each version was installed, over the same number of days after release, with counts; changed ratings move to the version at the change, so state that rule and show it. (4) Remove the rating from current state and the summaries, delete the review text, keep the developer's response only if policy allows (usually removed with the review), and keep only non-identifying aggregates.

Rubric anchors. 2: an append-only table with averages computed on read, no handling of changes, removals or resets. 3: current state with ordered updates, per-star counts updated by deltas, resets as a filter, removals as reversible state, per-version attribution defined. 4: also a rebuild and verification path, privacy of customer ids, hot-app handling, and credible answers for both incidents.

Strong signals. Asks what happens to a changed rating's version before drawing anything; keeps summaries as counts, not averages. Red flags. "Store the average and update it"; hard deletes for moderation; descriptions of how a real app store computes its ratings.

APL-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Catalogue. subscription_groups (group_id, name); products (product_id, group_id, level, duration P1M|P1Y|…, family_shareable); product_prices (product_id, storefront, currency, price_minor, valid_from, valid_to). Levels are attributes of products, versioned if the developer re-ranks (product_levels (product_id, level, valid_from)), because a move between levels is judged by the ranking in force when it happened.
  • Raw notifications. store_notifications (notification_id UNIQUE, type, subtype, original_transaction_id, transaction_id, signed_at, received_at, payload). Append-only, deduplicated by notification id; this is the evidence everything else is rebuilt from.
  • Chain. subscription_chains (chain_id, original_transaction_id UNIQUE, customer_key, group_id, storefront, first_purchase_at). One chain per customer and group in this exercise.
  • Billing periods. billing_periods (period_id, chain_id, transaction_id, product_id, level, period_start, period_end, offer_type NULL intro|promo, offer_id NULL, price_minor, currency, kind trial|paid, ended_reason renewed|upgraded|expired|refunded|revoked, revoked_at NULL). An exclusion constraint (or a scheduled check) enforces no overlap per chain. An upgrade closes the old period at the upgrade instant (ended_reason upgraded) and opens a new one there.
  • Scheduled changes. scheduled_changes (change_id, chain_id, from_product, to_product, kind downgrade|crossgrade, chosen_at, effective_at, status pending|applied|cancelled). It becomes a period only at renewal.
  • Money events. subscription_money (money_id, chain_id, period_id, kind charge|proration_refund|refund, amount_minor signed, currency, occurred_at). Proration and refunds are rows, never edits to a period's price.
  • Offers. offer_redemptions (chain_id, customer_key, group_id, offer_type, offer_id, period_id, redeemed_at) plus eligibility_decisions (customer_key, group_id, offer_id, decided_at, eligible, reason, evidence_redemption_id NULL). Intro eligibility = no intro redemption by the customer in the group.
  • Family access. shared_entitlements (shared_id, purchaser_chain_id, member_key, valid_from, valid_to, ended_reason). Its validity is bounded by the purchaser's entitlement; no money rows ever reference it.
  • Facts. fct_entitlement_daily (date, chain_id or member_key, role purchaser|family, product_id, level, storefront, paid flag) derived from periods and shared entitlements (end-of-day or "any time in the day" — stated); fct_level_moves (month, chain_id, from_level, to_level, kind, effective_at); fct_offer_conversion (offer_id, storefront, cohort month, converted_by_day_n); fct_revenue_daily from money events (recognised over the period, proration refunds as negative recognition).

Competing designs to accept. Event-sourcing the chain from notifications with periods as a projection (if the projection is rebuildable and ordered by signed date, not arrival). A single "subscription state history" table with valid_from/valid_to per chain instead of periods, if scheduled changes and money stay separate. Treating family members as entitlements on the purchaser's chain rather than separate rows, if they are countable and carry no revenue.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A current-level column overwritten on each notification; applying a downgrade on the day it is chosen; counting trials as paid; intro eligibility per product; summing currencies; revenue on cash date instead of recognised over the period; family members in revenue-per-subscriber denominators; out-of-order notifications applied in arrival order; rebuilding the daily snapshot for all {{subscribers}} chains every night instead of only chains with new notifications.

Incident guidance.

  • Overlapping periods from out-of-order upgrade notifications: contain by marking the affected chains and excluding the overlap from per-level counts (keep the later-signed period for each instant); fix by rebuilding those chains' periods from the stored notifications in signed-date order; guard with an overlap check per chain and a reconciliation that Σ per-level actives = total actives across the {{levels}} levels, which would have paged on day one.
  • Intro offer granted twice after crossgrades: eligibility keyed by product instead of group. Fix the key to (customer, group); list affected customers from redemptions in all {{storefronts}} storefronts; decide with the business whether to honour the grants (usually yes) and record them as exceptions; add a test that a crossgrade never changes eligibility.
  • Revenue per subscriber dropped by about {{family_share}}: the denominator changed definition, not the business. Restore the purchaser-only denominator, publish family members as their own metric, annotate the chart, and require a metric definition version on every dashboard tile.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Trial period (kind trial, intro offer), paid period at level 3, upgrade on day 10: the level-3 period ends at the upgrade instant with a pro-rata refund row; a full level-1 period starts then; the downgrade is a pending scheduled change that becomes a level-2 period at the next renewal. (2) Paid and entitled at end of day (or any time in the day), excluding trials and family members; a refund revokes from the refund time — past days stay counted, and if the business wants refunded periods excluded retroactively that is a labelled restatement. (3) A move counts when it takes effect; a crossgrade to a yearly product at the same level is a crossgrade (level unchanged), effective at renewal. (4) Snapshot per day from periods with an interval join; only chains with notifications since the last run are rebuilt; a late notification rebuilds that chain's days and the affected daily aggregates. (5) Family access ends when the purchaser's entitlement ends (refund, expiry); a downgrade to a non-shareable product ends it at renewal; revenue per subscriber uses purchasers only.

Rubric anchors. 2: one subscriptions table with a current product and status, trials counted as paid, downgrades applied immediately. 3: chain / periods / notifications separated, non-overlapping periods, scheduled changes, intro eligibility per group, money as events, a defined paid-subscriber count. 4: also out-of-order handling by signed date, revocation semantics and restatement, family access without revenue, incremental rebuilds, and each incident guarded.

Strong signals. Asks what "active" means at an instant before drawing tables; distinguishes billing from entitlement; notices that eligibility is a group-level fact. Red flags. Updating the period's price to apply proration; deriving levels from product names; trusting arrival order of notifications.

APL-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Identity. devices (device_key, serial, model_id, configuration, manufactured_at); device_replacements (old_device_key, new_device_key, case_id, replaced_at); models (model_id, family, release_date).
  • Intervals (bitemporal). Each table carries valid_from, valid_to (when it was true) and recorded_from, recorded_to (when we believed it):
    • device_ownership (device_key, owner_key, valid_from, valid_to, start_event_id, end_event_id, recorded_from, recorded_to); owner_key is pseudonymous; the identity mapping lives in a separate, access-controlled store.
    • part_installations (device_key, slot display|battery|camera|main_board|…, part_serial, part_condition new|refurbished|harvested, valid_from, valid_to, event_id, recorded_from, recorded_to).
    • coverage (device_key, plan_id, valid_from, valid_to, transferred_from_device_key NULL, recorded_from, recorded_to).
  • Events. lifecycle_events (event_id, device_key, type activation|transfer|repair|whole_unit_replacement|trade_in|refurbishment|resale|retire, occurred_at, source, source_record_id, received_at); repairs (repair_id, event_id, provider_id, under_coverage, parts_replaced). Late records are inserted with their true occurred_at and a later recorded time.
  • Constraints. No overlapping valid intervals per (device, slot) and per part_serial (current recorded version); one owner per device at any valid time. Enforced by exclusion constraints or a nightly checker on current rows.
  • Facts. fct_device_month (month, device_key, model, age_months, in_use, refurbished_flag); fct_repairs (repair_id, device_key, model, age_at_repair, slot, under_coverage, occurred_at, recorded_at). The battery replacement rate per 1,000 in-use devices by model and age band uses the month's in-use devices as the denominator; published months are snapshots tagged with the recorded-time cut-off they used.
  • Privacy. Analysts see owner_key only; erasure deletes the identity mapping (and any personal attributes), so ownership intervals remain as "an owner" with an unlinkable key.

Competing designs to accept. An event log as the source of truth with materialised current and historical interval tables (if rebuildable and checked). Uni-temporal intervals plus a separate audit table of corrections, if "as known on" queries can be reproduced. A graph model (device–part–owner edges with time), if the non-overlap rules are enforced.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Owner and part columns on the device row (history lost); late records overwriting intervals; parts keyed by slot without the part serial (cannot detect a part in two devices); whole-unit replacement treated as a new customer device with no link; erasure deleting history; monthly rates recomputed silently after backfills; interval tables at {{devices}} devices queried without indexing on (device, valid range).

Incident guidance.

  • Repair feed down for {{late_record_days}} days: contain by flagging the affected weeks as incomplete for that provider (feed freshness per source on the dashboard); after the backfill publish the restated rate next to the original with the recorded-time cut-off; guard with a completeness check (expected vs received records per provider per day) before a weekly number is used in a review.
  • A display serial in two devices: the harvest did not close the source installation. Close the old interval at the harvest time (as a new recorded version), re-run the overlap checker, and make the refurbishment workflow write "remove from A" and "install in B" as one transaction; add the per-part-serial overlap check to the pipeline gate.
  • Erasure deleted ownership intervals: restore the intervals from backup or the event log with a fresh unlinkable owner key; fix the erasure job to delete the identity mapping only; add a test that the next owner's coverage check still sees prior repairs after an erasure, run in all {{markets}} markets' configurations.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Ownership A then B then C as intervals; battery and display installations with part serials; the harvested display gets a closing interval in this device and an opening one in the other; trade-in ends B's ownership; refurbishment adds a new display interval; resale opens C. (2) The late repair adds a row with an earlier valid time and a later recorded time; last month's published rate (recorded cut-off) stays; the restated rate is published beside it. (3) A replacement link carries case history and coverage to the new serial; devices in use counts the new serial and retires the old; age can be reported from the original purchase for warranty and from manufacture for quality. (4) Delete the identity mapping and personal attributes; keep intervals with an unlinkable key; C's claim still sees the repair. (5) Devices × slots × a few installations each: billions of rows at the top level; partition by device hash, index (device_key, slot, valid range), keep a current-parts table for support reads.

Rubric anchors. 2: one devices table with owner and parts columns updated in place. 3: identity separated from intervals, part serials, events, non-overlap rules, pseudonymous owners. 4: also bitemporal recording, restatement policy, replacement links, erasure that preserves history, and each incident guarded.

Strong signals. Asks "true when versus known when" unprompted; puts the part serial, not the slot, at the centre of part history. Red flags. Storing owner names in analytics tables; deleting history on erasure; inferring "in use" from device signals the scenario never provides.

APL-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Entities with internal keys. works (work_id, title, iswc NULL); recordings (recording_id, title, version_type original|remaster|live|radio_edit|clean|…, duration_ms, audio_fingerprint NULL, work_id NULL); releases (release_id, type album|single|ep|compilation|deluxe, upc, release_date, source_id); tracks (track_id, release_id, disc, position, recording_id, valid_from, valid_to); artists (artist_id, name); credits (recording_id, artist_id, role primary|featured|remixer, ordinal).
  • Source evidence. source_identifiers (entity_type, entity_id, scheme isrc|upc|iswc|source_native, value, source_id, delivery_id, confidence). ISRC and UPC are attributes with provenance, never primary keys: one ISRC can (wrongly) label two audio files, and one recording can carry two ISRCs.
  • Deliveries. deliveries (delivery_id, source_id, received_at, kind new|update|takedown) and versioned catalogue rows (valid_from/valid_to) so a takedown ends availability, not existence.
  • Identity layers. recording_clusters (cluster_id) with recording_cluster_map (recording_id, cluster_id, valid_from, valid_to, decided_by, evidence) for duplicates of the same audio; song_map (cluster_id, song_id, valid_from, valid_to) grouping versions (original, remaster, live) of one work by one primary artist. Merges and splits close and open map rows; nothing is deleted.
  • Plays. fct_play (play_id, played_at, listener_key, track_id, …) at event grain, partitioned by day; it stores what was played (track_id) and nothing derived. Daily aggregates agg_track_day (day, track_id, plays) are cheap to keep.
  • Rollups. recording plays = Σ over tracks of that recording; cluster plays through the map valid at report time (or at play time — a stated choice); song plays through song_map; release plays via track.release_id; artist plays = plays of recordings credited to the artist (each credited artist gets the full play). Totals across artists are never computed by summing artist counts; "total plays" comes from the play fact.
  • Finality. A month's artist report is a published snapshot with the map version (or valid time) it used. Later merges apply going forward and, if material, through a documented restatement with deltas.

Competing designs to accept. Resolving cluster and song ids at ingestion into the play row (fast reads) with a re-key job on merges, if the original track id is kept and restatement is explicit. A graph store for identity with a relational play fact. Weighted artist allocation (1/n per credit) for revenue-like metrics, if counts per artist still give each artist the full play.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. ISRC as primary key; denormalising song and artist into each play at {{daily_plays}} a day so merges require rewriting billions of rows; joins to credits multiplying plays in summaries; published months read through the current map; duplicates from {{sources}} sources splitting a song's plays; takedowns deleting rows that old reports reference.

Incident guidance.

  • Merge of about {{dup_share}} of recordings changed last month: the rollup read the current mapping. Re-publish last month from its snapshot (or from the map as of the publish time); apply the merge from its valid time; publish a restatement only if the policy says so. Guard: published reports pin the map version, and a diff check runs before any merge goes live.
  • Radio edits under album ISRCs: identifiers were trusted over audio. Split the recordings (new recording ids for the edits, using duration or fingerprint evidence), re-point the compilation's tracks, recompute affected song and chart numbers from the track-grain aggregates, and add a check that flags one ISRC mapped to audio of differing durations.
  • Artist totals exceed total plays: a credit join was summed across artists. Recompute the label summary from the play fact (distinct plays), fence the per-artist table with a "do not sum" contract or a role filter (primary only for totals), and add a reconciliation of the summary against total plays.

Follow-up guidance. (1) One work, recordings: original (on single, album and compilation tracks) and remaster (on the deluxe track); 10 plays → recording counts split original/remaster, song count 10, release counts per release. (2) Last month stays as published (or restated with deltas); this month uses the merged cluster from the merge's valid time. (3) Each of the three artists shows the full plays; total plays is the play count, not the sum (which would be 3×). (4) Store the track id; resolve at query time through versioned maps, with daily track-grain aggregates so a merge re-aggregates small tables, not the play log. (5) Detect by duration/fingerprint mismatch under one ISRC; split recordings and recompute from track aggregates.

Rubric anchors. 2: one songs table keyed by ISRC, plays joined to it, merges by rewriting. 3: work/recording/release/track separated, internal keys, identifiers as evidence, plays at track grain, versioned mapping for clusters. 4: also song-level grouping distinct from duplicate clusters, credit fan-out fenced, published-month pinning and restatement, and each incident guarded.

Strong signals. Separates "same audio" from "same song" without prompting; keeps the play log immutable. Red flags. Summing per-artist counts into totals; deleting merged recordings; assuming ISRCs are unique and correct.

APL-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Entities. apps (app_id, developer_id); app_versions (version_id, app_id, platform, version_string, created_at); builds (build_id, version_id, build_number, uploaded_at) with UNIQUE (version_id, build_number); submissions (submission_id, app_id, created_at, submitted_at, expedite_requested_at NULL); submission_items (submission_id, item_type app_version|in_app_purchase|in_app_event, item_id, build_id NULL); one build per platform per submission.
  • State history. submission_transitions (transition_id UNIQUE, submission_id, from_state, to_state, at, actor_type developer|reviewer|system, recorded_at). Append-only, deduplicated by transition id; states are a reference table with a "clock category" (waiting, in_review, with_developer, terminal) so a rename upstream changes a mapping row, not the metric.
  • Review episodes. review_episodes (episode_id, submission_id, version_id, entered_queue_at, review_started_at, decided_at, decision approved|rejected|metadata_rejected|developer_removed, is_first_for_version, expedited), derived from transitions. A metadata-only fix opens a new episode of the same submission; a new build means a new submission linked by resubmission_of.
  • Decisions. rejection_citations (episode_id, guideline_ref) many-to-many; messages (message_id, submission_id, sender_type, sent_at, content_ref) stored as references only.
  • Facts. fct_review_episode (one row per episode: wait_hours = review_started − entered_queue; review_hours = decided − review_started; expedited flag; queue-entry week and decision week); fct_version_outcome (one row per version: first submission, approval, episodes, resubmissions, total hours with time-with-developer separated).
  • Published statistic. For a week (by decision date, say), the 90th percentile of (decided_at − entered_queue_at) over non-expedited, non-removed episodes, published with the cohort definition; a week is final after its last episode decides or after a cut-off with open episodes reported.
  • Access. Developer views filter by developer_id and expose decisions, citations and their messages; reviewer ids exist only in restricted tables and never in published statistics.

Competing designs to accept. A state machine per submission with SCD2 rows instead of a transitions table, if durations derive from them. Treating each metadata fix as a new submission, if the link and first-pass rules are explicit. Percentiles via approximate sketches for the platform view, if published numbers are reproducible from stored episodes.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A status column overwritten; averages over skewed durations; first-pass defined per submission; guideline counts summed as rejections; durations tied to raw state names; expedited reviews mixed into the published wait time; duplicate transitions doubling durations; recomputing all history weekly at {{submissions_per_week}} a week instead of incrementally by episode.

Incident guidance.

  • Median time in review doubled after a rename: the duration job keyed on raw state names. Contain by withdrawing or annotating the published number; map the new state into the clock-category table; recompute the affected weeks for {{platforms}} platforms; guard with a check that every observed state has a category, failing the job on an unknown state.
  • First-pass rejection rate collapsed below the usual {{rejection_share}}: metadata fixes arrived as new submissions and were treated as first passes. Re-link them as episodes of the original submission (by app, version and timing); recompute first pass per version; add a test that each version has exactly one first episode.
  • Expedited reviews flatter waiting time: publish waiting time for standard reviews (excluding the normally ~{{expedite_share}} expedited) and report expedited volume beside it; alert when the expedited share departs from its baseline.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Submission 1 (build 41): episode 1 rejected with two citations; developer reply; submission 2 (build 42, resubmission_of 1): episode 2 metadata_rejected, episode 3 approved, held then released; durations from transitions with with-developer time separated. (2) A stated percentile (e.g. 90th) of queue-entry to decision for standard episodes, by decision week, final after a cut-off. (3) Denominator = versions whose first episode reached a decision; developer-removed before review excluded and reported separately; a metadata fix after a rejection means the first pass was a rejection. (4) Developer history straight from per-developer partitions of episodes; platform percentiles from the episode fact per week, computed incrementally. (5) Exclude or separate expedited episodes from the published standard wait; show both.

Rubric anchors. 2: one submissions table with a status and timestamps per status, averages. 3: version / build / submission / episode separated, append-only transitions, durations by event pairs, rates with denominators, guideline citations many-to-many. 4: also clock categories robust to renames, first-pass per version, percentile definition with finality, expedite handling, developer-scoped views without reviewer identity, and each incident guarded.

Strong signals. Defines each duration as an event pair before drawing tables; asks about the denominator of every rate. Red flags. Averages for skewed durations; reviewer identity in developer views; counting guideline citations as rejections.

APL-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{report_end}} is the instance's report end date)

WITH rel AS (                                   -- one phased release per app, with the phased build
  SELECT l.app_id, l.action_date AS start_date, b.build_number AS phased_build
  FROM phased_release_log l
  JOIN app_builds b ON b.app_id = l.app_id AND b.version = l.version
  WHERE l.action = 'start'
), cal AS (                                     -- every date from the start to the report end
  SELECT r.app_id, g::date AS activity_date
  FROM rel r
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(r.start_date::timestamp, TIMESTAMP '{{report_end}}', INTERVAL '1 day') AS g
), st AS (                                      -- state from the latest action on or before the date
  SELECT c.app_id, c.activity_date,
         CASE a.action WHEN 'pause' THEN 'paused' WHEN 'release_all' THEN 'complete' ELSE 'active' END AS release_state
  FROM cal c
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT l.action FROM phased_release_log l
    WHERE l.app_id = c.app_id AND l.action_date <= c.activity_date
    ORDER BY l.action_date DESC
    LIMIT 1
  ) a
), ph AS (                                      -- phase_day counts active dates only
  SELECT app_id, activity_date, release_state,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE release_state = 'active')
           OVER (PARTITION BY app_id ORDER BY activity_date) AS phase_day
  FROM st
), win AS (                                     -- the release ends at day 7 or release_all
  SELECT ph.*,
         MIN(activity_date) FILTER (WHERE release_state = 'complete' OR phase_day = 7)
           OVER (PARTITION BY app_id) AS end_date
  FROM ph
), dev AS (                                     -- one row per app, local date and device
  SELECT s.app_id, (s.started_at AT TIME ZONE a.report_tz)::date AS activity_date, s.device_id,
         BOOL_OR(b.build_number >= r.phased_build) AS on_new
  FROM app_sessions s
  JOIN apps a       ON a.app_id = s.app_id
  JOIN app_builds b ON b.app_id = s.app_id AND b.version = s.app_version
  JOIN rel r        ON r.app_id = s.app_id
  GROUP BY s.app_id, 2, s.device_id
)
SELECT w.app_id, w.activity_date, w.phase_day, w.release_state,
       CASE WHEN w.release_state = 'complete' THEN 100 ELSE ps.release_pct END AS release_pct,
       COUNT(d.device_id) AS active_devices,
       COUNT(d.device_id) FILTER (WHERE d.on_new) AS devices_on_new,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(d.device_id) FILTER (WHERE d.on_new) / NULLIF(COUNT(d.device_id), 0), 2) AS share_on_new
FROM win w
JOIN phase_schedule ps ON ps.phase_day = w.phase_day
LEFT JOIN dev d ON d.app_id = w.app_id AND d.activity_date = w.activity_date
WHERE w.activity_date <= COALESCE(w.end_date, DATE '{{report_end}}')
GROUP BY w.app_id, w.activity_date, w.phase_day, w.release_state, ps.release_pct
ORDER BY w.app_id, w.activity_date;

Explanation. The output is a calendar, not a summary of sessions, so it starts from a date spine built from each app's start date; dates with no sessions and paused dates then appear by construction. The state of a date is the latest action on or before it. phase_day is a running count of active dates, which is exactly why a paused date holds the percentage and pushes the end of the release later. The end date depends on that running count, so it is found with a window over the finished calendar and applied as a filter afterwards (a WHERE before the window would change the count). Sessions are reduced to one row per app, local date and device with BOOL_OR over "build_number ≥ the phased build", so a device that updated mid-day counts once and as updated, and a hotfix build counts as the new code. COUNT(d.device_id) (not COUNT(*)) gives 0 on a date with no devices, and NULLIF turns its share into NULL. The comparison uses build numbers because version strings do not sort as text ('2.9.6' > '2.10.0').

Complexity. The spine is (apps × days); the LATERAL lookup is one index probe per date on (app_id, action_date). The session pass is one hash aggregate to device-day grain, which dominates. In production the device-day rollup (app, date, device, max build) is computed once per day and this report reads only that, so it is days × devices, not sessions.

Dialect notes. Not executed here. Snowflake: GENERATOR/ROW_NUMBER or a calendar table for the spine, CONVERT_TIMEZONE(report_tz, started_at)::DATE, BOOLOR_AGG, COUNT_IF, IFF; a correlated "latest action" is usually written as ASOF JOIN or QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() … = 1. BigQuery: GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY + UNNEST, DATE(started_at, report_tz), LOGICAL_OR, COUNTIF, SAFE_DIVIDE; window COUNTIF(...) OVER (...). Spark SQL: sequence(start, end, interval 1 day) + explode, to_date(from_utc_timestamp(started_at, report_tz)), bool_or, count_if. MySQL 8: a recursive CTE for the spine, CONVERT_TZ (needs time zone tables loaded), no FILTER clause (use SUM(CASE …)), and no LATERAL before 8.0.14.

Edge cases built into the data. A paused date (and at Very Hard two pauses, up to three days long); a session at exactly local midnight and one at 23:59:59; devices with several sessions in a day and devices that updated mid-day; manual updaters ahead of the schedule; sessions the day before the start and after the end; the report end after the release finished (Medium) so rows must stop at phase day 7. Hard adds several apps, a release_all (with or without an earlier pause), an app whose release is cut by the report end, a date with no sessions at all, and devices shared across apps. Very Hard adds per-app time zones (east and west of UTC, sometimes a half-hour offset), a hotfix build after the phased build including a device seen only on the hotfix, and version strings whose text order disagrees with build order.

Common mistakes. Counting sessions instead of devices; numbering dates since the start so pauses advance the phase; integer division (100 * on / active with integers truncates); not stopping at phase day 7 or release_all; (Hard+) starting from sessions or using an inner join so empty dates vanish, or COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN, which returns 1 for an empty date; (Very Hard) app_version = phased version (misses the hotfix), comparing version strings as text, and UTC dates instead of the report time zone. Each has a diagnostic except COUNT(*), which shows as a wrong count on the empty date.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Add per-day crash-free session share by build (another fact joined at device-day grain); the phased cohort is not random: automatic-update users differ from manual updaters, and early days are tiny, so compare with confidence intervals and against the same days of previous releases. (2) Devices that updated before the schedule could reach them, or whose sessions show the new build on a day when the cumulative share far exceeds release_pct, point to manual updates; per-device eligibility is not in the data, so the split is only an estimate. (3) Keep a daily device-version rollup (app, date, device, max build); a late session updates that rollup and a published day is either restated with a version or frozen after a cut-off — state which. (4) Count active phase days (not calendar days) to 90%, or report both; exclude or annotate releases that went to release_all early.

Rubric anchors. 2: a share per date from sessions, but pauses advance the phase or empty dates vanish. 3: matches the expected result at the level asked. 4: also explains why phase days skip pauses, the device-day rollup for scale, and the selection bias of the phased cohort.

Strong signals. Builds the date spine first without being told; reduces to device-day grain before counting; compares builds numerically. Red flags. MAX(app_version) as text; COUNT(*) after the LEFT JOIN; filtering the end date before computing the running count.
APL-L3-05.reference_sql:
WITH rel AS (                                   -- one phased release per app, with the phased build
  SELECT l.app_id, l.action_date AS start_date, b.build_number AS phased_build
  FROM phased_release_log l
  JOIN app_builds b ON b.app_id = l.app_id AND b.version = l.version
  WHERE l.action = 'start'
), cal AS (                                     -- every date from the start to the report end
  SELECT r.app_id, g::date AS activity_date
  FROM rel r
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(r.start_date::timestamp, TIMESTAMP '{{report_end}}', INTERVAL '1 day') AS g
), st AS (                                      -- state from the latest action on or before the date
  SELECT c.app_id, c.activity_date,
         CASE a.action WHEN 'pause' THEN 'paused' WHEN 'release_all' THEN 'complete' ELSE 'active' END AS release_state
  FROM cal c
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT l.action FROM phased_release_log l
    WHERE l.app_id = c.app_id AND l.action_date <= c.activity_date
    ORDER BY l.action_date DESC
    LIMIT 1
  ) a
), ph AS (                                      -- phase_day counts active dates only
  SELECT app_id, activity_date, release_state,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE release_state = 'active')
           OVER (PARTITION BY app_id ORDER BY activity_date) AS phase_day
  FROM st
), win AS (                                     -- the release ends at day 7 or release_all
  SELECT ph.*,
         MIN(activity_date) FILTER (WHERE release_state = 'complete' OR phase_day = 7)
           OVER (PARTITION BY app_id) AS end_date
  FROM ph
), dev AS (                                     -- one row per app, local date and device
  SELECT s.app_id, (s.started_at AT TIME ZONE a.report_tz)::date AS activity_date, s.device_id,
         BOOL_OR(b.build_number >= r.phased_build) AS on_new
  FROM app_sessions s
  JOIN apps a       ON a.app_id = s.app_id
  JOIN app_builds b ON b.app_id = s.app_id AND b.version = s.app_version
  JOIN rel r        ON r.app_id = s.app_id
  GROUP BY s.app_id, 2, s.device_id
)
SELECT w.app_id, w.activity_date, w.phase_day, w.release_state,
       CASE WHEN w.release_state = 'complete' THEN 100 ELSE ps.release_pct END AS release_pct,
       COUNT(d.device_id) AS active_devices,
       COUNT(d.device_id) FILTER (WHERE d.on_new) AS devices_on_new,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(d.device_id) FILTER (WHERE d.on_new) / NULLIF(COUNT(d.device_id), 0), 2) AS share_on_new
FROM win w
JOIN phase_schedule ps ON ps.phase_day = w.phase_day
LEFT JOIN dev d ON d.app_id = w.app_id AND d.activity_date = w.activity_date
WHERE w.activity_date <= COALESCE(w.end_date, DATE '{{report_end}}')
GROUP BY w.app_id, w.activity_date, w.phase_day, w.release_state, ps.release_pct
ORDER BY w.app_id, w.activity_date;

APL-L4-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Use-case registry: each approved use case has an id, the value domain, the mechanism and its parameters (ε = {{epsilon}} per report), allowed slicing attributes, retention, and an owner. The device downloads the signed registry; a use case not in it cannot report.
  • On the device: the value is chosen from local data. For a small domain, generalised randomised response: report the true value with probability p = e^ε / (e^ε + k − 1), otherwise one of the other k − 1 values uniformly. For a large domain ({{domain_size}} values) that is useless (p is tiny), so the device hashes the value with a randomly chosen hash function into a small range and randomises that (local hashing), or encodes it into a sketch row (count-mean or Hadamard-style), sending the hash index with the noisy bits. The error then depends on ε and n, not on the domain size.
  • Per-day limit: a ledger in protected storage on the device counts reports per rolling 24 hours across all use cases ({{reports_per_day}} at most). Budget is spent when the randomised report is created, not when it is uploaded. The randomised report is stored in the upload queue and resent byte-identical on every retry; if the queue overflows, reports are dropped, never regenerated. The window uses stored creation times and does not reset when the wall clock moves backwards (a strong answer also mentions memoising the randomised answer for a value that does not change from day to day, so repeating it does not leak more over time).
  • Ingestion: a dedicated endpoint whose front end drops network addresses and transport metadata before anything is stored or logged. The envelope holds only the use-case id, a coarse client version, the day, the payload and a fresh random report id used solely to drop retried duplicates. No device, account or persistent id. Reports are batched and stored by day; raw reports are deleted after 30 days.
  • Aggregation: a daily batch per use case counts the noisy reports, debiases them (for randomised response, estimate = (observed − n·q) / (p − q), with q the probability of reporting any particular other value), decodes the sketch for dictionary values, and computes a standard error for each estimate. For local hashing the variance is about n · 4e^ε / (e^ε − 1)²: at n = 100 million and ε = 2 the standard error is about 8,500, so true counts below a few tens of thousands cannot be told from zero.
  • Release rules: publish only values whose estimate exceeds a threshold of several standard errors (higher when many values are compared, to control false "top values"), only for populations above a floor, only for approved coarse slices, always with intervals. Product teams get tables of released estimates, never raw reports.
  • Governance and proof: a review approves each use case's ε, slices and share of the daily budget; devices pick at most {{reports_per_day}} eligible use cases per day at random. Proof that the limit held comes from client tests, a lab fleet of test devices whose sends are captured, and a server monitor of reports per day per client version against the expected count for that version's opted-in population.

Competing designs to accept. Plain randomised response for a small domain if the candidate shows the domain is small. Count-mean sketch, Hadamard response or local hashing for a large one. A shuffler or anonymising relay between devices and the server, if the candidate explains what it adds and whom it trusts. Discovering new values with fragment- or prefix-based heavy-hitter rounds, as long as each round is charged to the daily limit.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Re-randomising on retry (averaging away the noise); budget enforced on the server (impossible without linking); identifying attributes added "for slicing"; transport metadata in somebody else's logs; tiny slices where noise dominates; a top-K over many noisy estimates that crowns noise; dictionary values that hide new popular values.

Incident guidance.

  • Fresh report per retry: k independent noisy copies of one value let an observer average the noise away, so those devices effectively spent about k·ε. Turn the use case off for that client version through the registry, delete the raw reports carrying that version since the release (they cannot be separated per device, by design), and publish nothing derived from them. Fix the client to persist and resend the randomised report, add a test that a retried upload is byte-identical, and alarm on reports per version exceeding {{reports_per_day}} times that version's expected population.
  • Negative counts in a 3,000-device slice: the standard error in that slice is of the same size as most true counts, and the largest of thousands of noisy estimates is mostly noise. Withdraw the table, explain why, and apply the release floor and thresholds; offer a coarser slice, several days pooled, or the value's interval instead.
  • Network addresses in another team's logs: treat it as a privacy incident. Stop the logging for this endpoint now, purge the logs, their replicas and backups, check who accessed them, and record the incident through the privacy owner. Prevention: a dedicated front end for the endpoint with its logging configuration under test, a periodic scan for addresses in any log tied to it, and an agreement with the team that runs the load balancer.

Follow-up guidance. Make the candidate compute one standard error with their numbers. Ask where the limit is enforced and how a retry behaves; a candidate who would deduplicate on a device id has missed the point. Push on what a product team receives for a value below threshold.

Rubric anchors. 2: "add noise on the server" or a device id for deduplication; no estimator; no limit enforcement. 3: on-device randomisation with a correct debiasing estimator, a large-domain strategy, a device-side ledger with resend-not-regenerate, metadata stripped at ingestion, thresholds on release. 4: also quantitative error at the stated n and ε, budget shared across use cases with governance, proof the limit held, discovery of new values within budget, and crisp handling of all three incidents.

Strong signals. Starts from the estimator and its error; names what must never be linkable. Red flags. Collecting raw values "temporarily"; slicing by many attributes; treating ε as a dial product teams can turn up when results are noisy.

APL-L4-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Capture: the device creates a play id (random) when playback starts and logs recording id, start time by device clock, seconds heard, offline flag, app version and account. Uploads are batched; retries resend the same play ids. The service stamps arrival time.
  • Ingestion: an append-only raw table (partitioned by arrival date) deduplicated on play id. A second check looks for different play ids with the same account, device, recording and start time, reported per app version as a duplicate rate.
  • Clock validation: a start time after arrival, or earlier than arrival minus {{offline_days}} days, is flagged; such plays are quarantined or clamped by a stated rule rather than silently dated.
  • Qualifying: seconds heard ≥ {{qualify_seconds}}; subscription valid at the play's start (an effective-dated subscription history); arrival within {{offline_days}} days of the play; territory from the account's effective-dated storefront history at the play's start; not excluded by fraud review. Exclusions are rows with their own recorded time, not deletions.
  • Aggregation: an incremental table of counts keyed by (play day, arrival day, territory, recording), with exclusions entered as negative counts on the day they were recorded. A statement for month M is the sum over play days in M and arrival days up to the cutoff ({{close_days}} days after month end), so every statement is an as-of query that can be rerun exactly. At the volumes here this avoids rescanning tens of billions of raw rows each month.
  • Statements: generated at the cutoff, mapped to rights holders with the catalogue version in force, stored as frozen, versioned artefacts together with their manifest (the cutoff, the catalogue version, counts and checksums per line).
  • Adjustments: each new statement also lists, for every earlier month still inside the adjustment window, current as-of-now counts minus everything already reported for that month, as lines that name the period. Nothing sent is ever edited.
  • Traceability: raw plays are append-only with arrival time, so any line can be re-derived down to its play ids; access for rights-holder audits uses those manifests.

Competing designs to accept. A lakehouse with time travel instead of arrival-day keys, if the candidate shows the as-of query and how long versions are kept. Holding suspected automated plays in a pending state that is not reported until cleared (fewer negative adjustments, later payments). Streaming ingestion with batch statements; a fully batch pipeline is fine at monthly cadence.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Retry duplicates with new ids; device clocks; storefront changes mid-month; late offline plays after the cutoff; fraud found after reporting; catalogue mapping changes between statements; rescanning raw data for each restatement.

Incident guidance.

  • Offline plays sent twice with different ids: confirm through the secondary duplicate rate by app version. Mark the duplicates as excluded (recorded now), so the current month is right before its cutoff and last month's correction appears as negative adjustment lines on the next statement. Fix the client, add the duplicate-rate monitor as a gate before each statement, and tell affected rights holders why the adjustment exists.
  • Rights holder shows 12% more: reconcile before changing anything. Produce a waterfall from all plays received to qualifying plays: short plays below {{qualify_seconds}} seconds, plays without a valid subscription, plays attributed to other territories by storefront, late offline plays not yet arrived, exclusions, and recordings counted under another release of the album. Only a defect found in your own pipeline changes the statement; otherwise send the explanation.
  • 40,000 automated accounts: record exclusions with today's recorded time; the open month is corrected before its cutoff and the three reported months get negative adjustment lines with a reason code. Keep the evidence for disputes. Prevention: earlier detection, and possibly a pending state for suspicious plays.

Follow-up guidance. Ask for the exact query behind one statement line and how it is rerun a year later. Probe the territory rule with a mid-month storefront change. Ask what the adjustment window is and what happens to a play that arrives after it.

Rubric anchors. 2: one table updated in place, statements rerun on demand and different each time, no play ids. 3: device play ids with idempotent ingestion, event and arrival time, effective-dated subscription and storefront, frozen statements and computed adjustments. 4: also an incremental as-of aggregate that scales, clock validation, secondary duplicate detection, reconciliation by reason, and precise handling of each incident.

Strong signals. Defines a statement as an as-of query before drawing the pipeline. Red flags. Editing sent statements; deleting fraudulent plays; dating plays by arrival.

APL-L4-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • What the server sees: account and device ids, client version, request type, number and size of records, opaque record ids, change tags or version vectors used for conflict detection, timestamps, outcome codes, and the network address of the request. It needs some of this to work; it does not need to keep all of it.
  • Minimisation: logs have an allowlist of typed fields and no free-text fields; unknown request fields are dropped before logging. Record ids are random, never derived from names. Network addresses are used for abuse protection and dropped or truncated within a short window. Analytics tables coarsen time (hour) and size (buckets). Ciphertext is padded to size buckets where exact size could reveal content (for example an attachment's length). Logs kept {{log_days}} days, then only aggregates.
  • Service metrics from metadata: server-side sync latency = time from a change being committed for one device to its delivery to another device of the same account (commit time to fetch time); push delay; conflict rate from version mismatches; failure rates by request type and client version; storage per account by size bucket and by record count; active devices per account (about {{devices_per_account}}).
  • Opt-in client telemetry: fixed, content-free schema, aggregated on the device per day: decryption failures (with the writer's client version, which travels as plaintext metadata in the record envelope), conflicts resolved, end-to-end sync durations as histograms. For sensitive counts, a local privacy mechanism and release thresholds.
  • Broken releases: staged client rollout with gates on decrypt-failure rate per writer version; the server keeps previous ciphertext versions for a short time so healthy clients can restore; the server can refuse writes from a bad client version (it sees the version).
  • Questions refused: anything about content. Offer instead an opt-in on-device aggregate under a privacy mechanism, with a minimum population, or a user research study with consent.
  • Deduplication: no cross-account deduplication of encrypted content: making identical plaintext produce identical ciphertext lets the server confirm who stores a known file. At most, deduplicate within one account under that account's keys.
  • Support: sees device list, last sync time per device, error codes and client versions, never content; recovery happens on the user's devices.

Competing designs to accept. Encrypting record types and change metadata too (better privacy, harder conflict handling and debugging) if the candidate states the cost. Relying on the server's view only and no client telemetry, if they show how a decryption bug would still be found (for example devices repeatedly re-fetching the same records). Differentially private client aggregates for some product questions.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Metadata that leaks content (sizes, timing, names in debug fields); clients as the only witness of corruption; opt-in bias in telemetry; support pressure to "just look"; storage growth that cannot be explained by inspecting content.

Incident guidance.

  • Records other devices cannot decrypt: the signal must come from clients: decrypt failures by writer version, or re-fetch loops visible on the server. Halt the rollout, have the server refuse or flag writes from that version, ship a fix, and let healthy clients restore the last good ciphertext versions. Prevention: decrypt-failure gates in the staged rollout and a cross-version compatibility test in the client release process.
  • Record names in logs for five days: strip the field at the front end now, purge the logs (and copies, replicas, derived datasets) for the period, review access, and record it through the privacy owner, who decides on any notification. Prevention: allowlisted log schemas, a check that rejects new fields from reaching logs without review, and scanning for name-like strings.
  • Storage 30% above forecast: work from shape, not content: growth by client version (a version history or retry bug writing duplicates), by account (a few accounts or everyone), by record count versus record size, and by retention of old versions. Usually a write-rate anomaly per client version gives it away.

Follow-up guidance. Have the candidate define sync latency with only observable timestamps. Ask what support can see. Push on the formatting-feature question: a strong candidate declines or proposes an opt-in on-device aggregate with thresholds, and says who approves it.

Rubric anchors. 2: plans to log or index content "for analytics", or ignores metadata leaks. 3: inventory and minimisation of metadata, service metrics from metadata, opt-in content-free client telemetry, staged rollouts with recoverable versions, refusal of content questions. 4: also padding and convergent-encryption trade-offs, decrypt failures tied to writer versions, a log-field allowlist enforced at the edge, opt-in bias acknowledged, and precise handling of each incident.

Strong signals. Starts with what the server sees and what it should forget. Red flags. "We can decrypt for support"; free-text debug fields; cross-user deduplication of encrypted files.

APL-L4-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Model: price points per currency (amounts in minor units with the currency's exponent: zero, two or three decimals). A product's base price (base storefront, price point) and every storefront price (generated or override, amount, currency, tax-inclusive flag, the FX rate version and tax rate version used, the generation run) are rows with a valid-from instant, a valid-to instant and a recorded-at time (bitemporal). Schedules are rows with future valid-from instants. Subscriptions add a per-subscriber price record and price-change application events.
  • Effective instant: a strong answer chooses one rule and makes it visible: for example local midnight in a time zone designated for each storefront (shown to the developer as an instant per storefront), or a single UTC instant shown in local time. Either is acceptable if stated; ambiguity is not.
  • Regeneration: an FX or tax update starts a batch that computes candidate prices, snaps them to each currency's price-point grid, diffs them with the current prices and applies guardrails: a change beyond a band (for example ±30%) or a ratio near 10 or 100 needs review; per-currency exponent tests; a canary storefront first. The approved set is published as a new version with a future valid-from, switched by a version pointer, so rollback is a pointer change.
  • Read path: a precomputed, replicated key-value view of (product, storefront) → current price, next scheduled price and its switch instant, with a version. Caches switch at the instant themselves without a refresh. The product page and checkout read the same view; checkout issues a price quote (id, amount, currency, tax, version, expiry of a few minutes) and charges the quote. A scheduled change inside a quote's life honours the quote.
  • Purchase record: immutable, carrying quote id, price row version, amount in minor units, currency, tax amount and tax rate version, FX version, storefront and instant. "What did this customer pay and why" is a lookup plus the bitemporal rows it points to. Proceeds reports are reproducible from purchase records and versioned commission rules.
  • Scale: reads at {{purchases_per_second}} purchases per second from replicated in-memory or key-value stores; regeneration writes millions of rows into a new version off the read path.

Competing designs to accept. Computing equalised prices on read from base price and rates (less storage, harder audit and caching), if every input is versioned. A single UTC switch instant, if communicated clearly. Honouring or not honouring a mistaken price as a business decision, if the candidate names the owner and the record that supports either choice.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Currency exponents; rounding to price-point grids; effective instants across time zones; stale caches at a switch; mass regeneration contending with reads; audits impossible after in-place updates; tax-inclusive and tax-exclusive storefronts handled the same way.

Incident guidance.

  • UTC switch: the rule was not local. Refund the difference to customers charged the new price before their local first; for the future, switch at each storefront's local midnight (or show developers the UTC instant in local time) and add a pre-publish check that lists the local switch time per storefront.
  • Prices 100 times too low: freeze publishing, move the version pointer back (minutes, because prices are versioned), and quantify the purchases from the purchase records. Whether to honour them, and how developers are made whole, is a business decision; the records support either. Prevention: per-currency exponent from a reference table, unit tests for zero- and three-decimal currencies, the ratio guardrail and a canary storefront.
  • Tax change in nine days: add a new tax rate version with its effective date; regenerate that storefront's tax-inclusive prices (or keep prices and accept lower proceeds, if that is the developer's setting) and publish with valid-from at the effective instant; past reports still show the old rate because each purchase recorded the tax rate version it used.

Follow-up guidance. Ask for the exact effective instant in two storefronts. Probe a checkout that straddles a switch. Ask how the system answers an auditor's question about a price three years ago.

Rubric anchors. 2: one price column per product and storefront, updated in place, floats for money. 3: bitemporal effective-dated prices and schedules, minor units with exponents, defined switch instants, versioned regeneration with guardrails, immutable purchase records. 4: also price quotes so the page and checkout agree, version-pointer rollback, canary publishing, reproducible proceeds, and precise handling of each incident.

Strong signals. Asks about currency exponents and the switch instant early. Red flags. Floating-point money; schedules applied by a cron job editing rows; no record of the rate versions behind a price.

APL-L4-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Storage and sync: samples are the truth, stored encrypted on the user's devices and synced between them; a strong answer keeps the server unable to read values (end-to-end encrypted sync) and computes on the devices. A sample carries id, type, start, end, value, unit, source, the device, the local UTC offset at its start, created time and a deletion tombstone.
  • Merge: per user, type and day, sweep over every sample boundary; for each elementary segment take the highest-priority source that covers it; its contribution is the sample's value times the segment's share of the sample's duration (even-spread assumption). Totals are recomputed for any day touched by a late sample, an edit, a deletion or a change to the priority list. Because the priority list itself syncs and the computation is deterministic, every device reaches the same total once synced.
  • Local days: each sample's local date comes from its stored offset; a sample crossing local midnight is split proportionally. Travel days can be 16 or 32 hours long; that is correct, and the interface can say so.
  • Sources: a new source starts at the lowest priority; the user can reorder. Samples identical in interval and value from two sources are flagged as likely copies.
  • Sharing: a grant row (recipient, data types out of {{share_types}}, granularity per type: totals or samples, visible-from date, granted at, revoked at). Data shared under a grant is encrypted to the recipient's keys; the owner's devices send updates while the grant is active. Revocation stops updates at once, rotates the grant's keys, deletes server-held copies, and instructs the recipient's devices to delete theirs when they next connect. Copies a recipient already exported cannot be recalled, and the interface says so.
  • Apps: per-type read and write permissions, enforced by the on-device store.
  • Deletion: tombstones sync; totals recompute; shared copies are updated or removed.

Competing designs to accept. Server-side storage and merging with strict access controls, if the candidate justifies why the server must read values and limits who can. Merging by "most granular source wins" instead of a priority list, if explained. Sharing only daily totals, never samples, to reduce exposure.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Summing overlapping sources; apps copying other sources' data; day boundaries computed in the wrong zone; recomputing whole histories on every change; revocation that cannot reach an offline device; deletions that miss derived totals or recipients.

Incident guidance.

  • A connected app doubles totals: the merge summed across sources or placed the new app above the watch. Recompute with the app at the lowest priority by default, detect identical intervals and values across sources, and tell the user which source was ignored. Prevention: lowest-priority default for new sources and a copy detector.
  • Travel days wrong: days were computed in the device's current zone (or UTC) instead of each sample's recorded offset. Store the offset, recompute the affected days from samples, and add tests for flights across many zones and samples crossing midnight.
  • Revoked access still visible on an offline phone: revocation reached the server and online devices but not the offline one until it reconnects. On reconnection the device must check grants before showing shared data and delete revoked data; key rotation stops new data at once. Tell the user honestly what revocation guarantees.

Follow-up guidance. Have the candidate merge a concrete hour with a partial overlap and give the numbers. Ask which component can read values and why. Push on what revocation promises.

Rubric anchors. 2: sums all sources, UTC days, sharing as a flag on the account. 3: priority-based interval merge with proration, recomputation of affected days, local days from stored offsets, grants with scope and revocation, a reasoned choice of where computation runs. 4: also deterministic cross-device agreement, encryption to recipients with key rotation on revocation, honest limits, deletion through to recipients, copy detection for new sources, and precise handling of each incident.

Strong signals. Treats totals as derived from samples and defines the day carefully. Red flags. Sending raw health data to a server "for analytics"; no answer for offline recipients; revocation that deletes the owner's own data.

APL-L5-01.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • The request without the reason: a precise ask (the field and its semantics, or the capacity in events per second and for how long, or the export's extension and its end date), the date, an estimate of what it costs the other team, what the candidate's team will do to reduce that cost, and what happens if it is late. All of that can be shared; only the purpose cannot.
  • Honesty: says plainly "I cannot share what this is for" and does not invent a reason. A strong candidate notes that a false reason is discovered at announcement and damages every later request.
  • Bringing people in: asks the sponsor to add the minimum set of people (usually one lead per team) through the project's process, with a short written case so the sponsor can decide quickly; accepts a refusal and works within it.
  • Making it worth their while: offers engineers to do part of the work in the other team's system under their review, flexibility on the shape of the change, or a commitment of help on something the other team needs.
  • Workarounds: weighs building around another team's system (launch risk, on-call ownership, removal after launch) and prefers a supported change; if a workaround is unavoidable, it is agreed with the owner and has an end date.
  • After the announcement: thanks the teams specifically, explains what they enabled, acknowledges the inconvenience of working blind, and removes temporary arrangements.
  • Real example: a request made with limited context (secrecy, a sensitive reorganisation, a security issue under embargo, or simply incomplete information), what the candidate chose to say and not say, and how it turned out.

Red flags. A cover story; hinting at the secret to win help; going around the sponsor's process; building on another team's system without telling them; treating the other teams' questions as obstruction.

Rubric anchors. 2: either leaks the purpose or invents one; or simply escalates. 3: precise, costed request shared openly without the purpose; honest refusal to explain; minimal disclosure through the sponsor; something offered in return. 4: also a well-judged workaround decision with ownership and removal, repair of the relationships after announcement, and a credible real example handled with integrity.

APL-L5-02.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • First days: one list of everything promised, with each stakeholder's actual need and date (day one, week one, month one), agreed with {{stakeholder}} and the launch lead. Classification by recoverability: raw event capture (with its schema and durability) must be right on day one; derived metrics, dashboards and backfills can follow if the raw data exists.
  • The gap as a measured risk: for volume gaps, a synthetic event generator and load tests at and beyond expected volume, finding the first limit; for missing validation or backfill, validation at capture that quarantines rather than drops, and a replay path from raw storage; for an untested join, a run on production-sized data and a simpler fallback number that does not need the join. A defined degraded mode for launch day if the fix is not ready (for example raw capture plus a sampled or delayed metric).
  • Cuts: made early, as one decision with each owner of a promised feature, through the person entitled to agree; each cut comes with when it will arrive and what the stakeholder gets meanwhile.
  • Launch day: runbooks, on-call, dashboards on the pipeline's own health, who may switch to the degraded mode, and a time by which first numbers will be available, announced in advance.
  • Status: reported against thresholds decided in advance (what makes it red), early, without optimism; a sustainable pace for the team.
  • Real example: a fixed-date delivery where scope gave, what was cut and why, how stakeholders were told, and the result on the day.

Red flags. "We'll work weekends"; cutting quality of raw capture to save a dashboard; cuts announced on launch day; reporting green until the week before; no fallback.

Rubric anchors. 2: tries to deliver everything by working harder. 3: recoverability-based prioritisation protecting raw capture, measured risk with load tests and a fallback, early open cuts through the right people, honest status. 4: also an explicit degraded mode with decision rights, a replay path for derived data, sustainable pace, and a credible real example with measured outcome.

APL-L5-03.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • Diagnosis: separate one-to-ones with each engineer to understand their position on direction, ownership and how they feel treated; looks at the evidence (design reviews, duplicated components, incidents) and talks to others affected. Separates three questions: technical direction, decision rights, working relationship.
  • Owning the gap: acknowledges that ownership of {{area}} was never defined and that this is the leader's responsibility.
  • Settling ownership: a written decision on who owns {{area}} (or a clear split with a boundary and a rule for changes crossing it), what the owner decides alone, what needs consultation, and how disagreement is raised and closed (for example a design review with a named decider and a time limit). The technical direction is decided on evidence, with both engineers' strongest points included and credited.
  • Bringing them together: a joint conversation after the one-to-ones, with a clear goal: agree the rule, not relitigate history. Expectations about behaviour in reviews stated directly.
  • Repairing damage: consolidating the duplicated work with both involved; restarting stalled reviews with the new decision rule; a conversation with any engineer who wanted to leave; stopping side-taking.
  • If one will not accept it: a direct conversation about disagree-and-commit and its limits; if behaviour continues, treat it as a performance matter with specific examples.
  • Measures: review cycle times, duplicated work stopped, the two collaborating on a concrete deliverable, team feedback.
  • Real example: a conflict the candidate dealt with, their own actions, what changed, and what they would do differently.

Red flags. Waiting for it to resolve itself; deciding the technical question by seniority or by who is louder; only a joint meeting with no preparation; treating the conflict as personality alone; threatening either engineer without evidence.

Rubric anchors. 2: "get them in a room" or "let them sort it out". 3: separate diagnosis, owns the missing definition, written ownership and decision rights, joint agreement, concrete repair. 4: also fair handling that keeps both engineers' strengths, a disagreement path with a decider, clear handling of continued relitigation, measures of resolution, and a credible real example with lessons.

APL-L5-04.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • First conversation: accepts the other team's reason, asks what is still possible and when, and proposes the smallest version of {{interface}} that unblocks the launch (fewer fields, a lower frequency, a file instead of an interface).
  • Options, priced: (a) the minimal version from the other team; (b) the candidate's engineers building it in the other team's codebase, with the other team's review, standards and agreement on who runs it after launch; (c) a temporary alternative source (the nightly report) with its differences measured and documented, a named owner and a removal date; (d) launching part of the reporting later. Each priced in engineer-weeks, risk and what it leaves behind.
  • Negotiation: offers something real (engineers, taking over a chore, flexibility on the shape); writes down what is agreed.
  • Escalation: if no agreement, goes to the shared director together with the other lead if possible, with two or three options, their costs and a recommendation; accepts the decision and plans around it.
  • Communication: tells stakeholders early which parts of the launch change; if developers are affected, says what they will see and when the full version arrives; never presents an approximate source as exact.
  • Prevention: dependency agreements with checkpoints, early warning signals, and contingency planned for critical dependencies.
  • Real example: a dependency that fell through, what the candidate negotiated, the option chosen and its outcome.

Red flags. Escalating first; blaming the other team; a temporary source with no owner or removal plan; quietly launching on approximate data; pressing engineers into the other codebase without the other team's agreement.

Rubric anchors. 2: complains or escalates with no options. 3: minimal ask, priced options, negotiation with something to offer, escalation with options and a recommendation, honest communication. 4: also ownership and removal plans for any temporary path, joint escalation, prevention through agreements with checkpoints, and a credible real example.

APL-L5-05.html:
What a strong answer contains.

  • Overview: a clear problem statement, who depended on the system, real numbers (volumes per day, peak to average, latency or freshness targets, data size, cost), the architecture at the right altitude, and the candidate's role.
  • Depth on the chosen angle: for the data model, keys, grain, how it handled change and late or corrected data, and why it held up; for correctness, the invariant at risk, how it was detected, the fix and the proof; for reliability, the failure guarded against, the mechanism, how it was tested and what it cost.
  • The privacy redesign for {{devices}} devices: names what moves onto the device (filtering, aggregation, randomisation), what leaves and in what form, and what the server may still know (counts, coarse attributes, no linkable identifiers). Recognises which outputs survive (population aggregates), which become estimates with error, and which are lost (per-user joins, funnels across sessions, long-term cohorts unless designed differently). Knows that hashing an identifier does not anonymise it.
  • The privacy feature: for raw events staying on the device, on-device aggregation with a fixed schema and server-side sums; for a per-day limit, enforcement on the device with a persisted ledger, since the server cannot link reports; for a release threshold, a minimum population and error-based thresholds with suppression; for deletion, lineage from every derived table back to the user's records, deletion propagated with verification, or aggregates that hold no per-user data. Accept other sound answers that fit their system, and do not expect deep differential-privacy mathematics.
  • Honesty: what failed, what they would change, what was the team's versus theirs, and which parts of the privacy answer are reasoning rather than experience.

How to judge. Probe numbers (per day or total? peak?), alternatives considered, and one failure in detail. A candidate who owned part of a system and says so precisely scores well; one who claims the whole system but cannot explain its keys or failure modes does not. In the privacy half, reward correct reasoning about what the server must not see over vocabulary.

Red flags. Only buzzwords; numbers that change under questioning; no failure ever; cannot say what they personally did; "we hash the user id, so it is anonymous"; claiming privacy with no change to what leaves the device.

Rubric anchors. 2: high-level description, vague numbers, no clear personal contribution, privacy treated as access control only. 3: clear framing with numbers, real depth on the chosen angle, honest failure story, a reasoned split between device and server with what is lost stated. 4: also alternatives with evidence, a verifiable path to the privacy feature, correct handling of identifiers and thresholds, crisp separation of own and team contributions, and lessons that show changed practice.
